summary.text: Letting \(d\) be the digit sum of \(n\), the congruence \(n\equiv d\pmod 9\) permits a choice of \(m\le n\) with \(d\mid n+9m\); eventual periodicity of powers of \(10\) modulo \(d\) then lets one place \(n-m\) digits \(1\) in one residue pattern and \(m\) digits \(1\) one position later, producing a multiple of \(d\) whose digit sum is exactly \(n\). Multiplying this number by a sufficiently large power of \(10\) preserves its digit sum and divisibility by \(d\), while making it distinct from \(n\), so it is a Harshad amicable partner.

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(x)\) denote the sum of the base-ten digits of the nonnegative integer \(x\). A positive integer \(k\neq n\) is a Harshad amicable partner of \(n\) when
\[
D(n)\mid k\qquad\text{and}\qquad D(k)\mid n.
\]
We prove that every positive integer \(n\) has such a partner. It will then follow immediately that the set from which \(a(n)\) is chosen is nonempty, so that \(a(n)\), being its least element, is positive and hence nonzero.

We first establish the main construction needed in the proof.

**Lemma.** Suppose that \(d,n\) are positive integers satisfying
\[
d\le n\qquad\text{and}\qquad \gcd(9,d)\mid n.
\]
Then there is a positive integer \(K\) such that
\[
d\mid K\qquad\text{and}\qquad D(K)=n.
\]

**Proof of the lemma.** We begin by choosing an auxiliary integer \(m\). Put
\[
g=\gcd(9,d).
\]
By hypothesis, write \(n=gq\). Bézout's identity supplies integers \(A,B\) such that
\[
g=9A+dB.
\]
Choose \(m\) to be the least nonnegative residue of \(-Aq\) modulo \(d\). Thus
\[
0\le m<d
\]
and \(m\equiv -Aq\pmod d\). Multiplying the Bézout identity by \(q\), we obtain
\[
n=gq=9Aq+dBq.
\]
Consequently,
\[
n+9m\equiv 9Aq+9(-Aq)\equiv0\pmod d.
\]
Therefore
\[
d\mid n+9m. \tag{1}
\]
Moreover, because \(m<d\le n\), we have \(m\le n\), so both \(n-m\) and \(m\) are nonnegative.

We next find a periodic portion of the sequence of powers of \(10\) modulo \(d\). There are only \(d\) residue classes modulo \(d\), whereas the list
\[
10^0,10^1,\ldots,10^d
\]
contains \(d+1\) terms. By the pigeonhole principle, two of these terms have the same residue. Hence there are integers \(t\ge0\) and \(L>0\) such that
\[
10^{t+L}\equiv10^t\pmod d. \tag{2}
\]
It follows by induction on \(i\ge0\) that
\[
10^{t+iL}\equiv10^t\pmod d. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, the assertion is immediate for \(i=0\). If it holds for \(i\), then
\[
10^{t+(i+1)L}=10^{t+iL}10^L
 \equiv10^t10^L
 =10^{t+L}
 \equiv10^t\pmod d,
\]
where the final congruence is (2).

For \(i=0,1,\ldots,n-1\), define an exponent
\[
e_i=t+iL+\varepsilon_i,
\]
where
\[
\varepsilon_i=
\begin{cases}
0,&i<n-m,\\
1,&i\ge n-m.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus the first \(n-m\) exponents have no extra shift, while the last \(m\) exponents are shifted upward by one.

The sequence \(e_0,e_1,\ldots,e_{n-1}\) is strictly increasing. In fact, the sequence \(\varepsilon_i\) is nondecreasing, and
\[
e_{i+1}-e_i=L+(\varepsilon_{i+1}-\varepsilon_i)\ge L\ge1.
\]
Now set
\[
K=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}10^{e_i}. \tag{4}
\]
Since the exponents are distinct, the decimal expansion of \(K\) has a digit \(1\) in each of the \(n\) positions \(e_0,\ldots,e_{n-1}\), and a digit \(0\) in every other position. There are no carries, precisely because no two summands use the same power of \(10\). It follows that
\[
D(K)=\underbrace{1+\cdots+1}_{n\text{ terms}}=n. \tag{5}
\]
Since \(n>0\), the sum (4) has at least one positive term, so \(K>0\).

It remains to prove that \(d\mid K\). For the first \(n-m\) indices, equation (3) gives
\[
10^{e_i}=10^{t+iL}\equiv10^t\pmod d.
\]
For the remaining \(m\) indices,
\[
10^{e_i}=10^{t+iL+1}\equiv10^{t+1}=10\cdot10^t\pmod d.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
K
&\equiv (n-m)10^t+m10^{t+1}\pmod d\\
&=10^t\bigl((n-m)+10m\bigr)\\
&=10^t(n+9m)\pmod d.
\end{aligned}
\]
By (1), \(d\mid n+9m\), so the final expression is congruent to zero modulo \(d\). Thus \(d\mid K\), completing the proof of the lemma.

We now apply the lemma to an arbitrary positive integer \(n\). Let
\[
d=D(n).
\]
We recall three elementary properties of decimal digit sums.

First, \(d>0\) because a positive integer has at least one nonzero decimal digit.

Second,
\[
D(n)\le n. \tag{6}
\]
For completeness, this follows by induction from the decimal decomposition \(n=10q+r\), where \(0\le r<10\). If \(q=0\), then \(n=r\) and \(D(n)=r=n\). If \(q>0\), then \(q<n\), and the induction hypothesis gives \(D(q)\le q\). Hence
\[
D(n)=D(q)+r\le q+r\le10q+r=n.
\]
Thus \(d\le n\).

Third, every integer is congruent modulo \(9\) to its decimal digit sum. Indeed, if
\[
n=\sum_j c_j10^j
\]
is its decimal expansion, then \(10\equiv1\pmod9\), and consequently
\[
n\equiv\sum_j c_j=D(n)=d\pmod9. \tag{7}
\]
Let
\[
g=\gcd(9,d).
\]
Since \(g\mid9\), congruence (7) also holds modulo \(g\), so \(n\equiv d\pmod g\). But \(g\mid d\), and therefore \(d\equiv0\pmod g\). It follows that
\[
n\equiv0\pmod g,
\]
or equivalently,
\[
\gcd(9,d)\mid n. \tag{8}
\]

The hypotheses of the lemma are now satisfied: \(d>0\), \(d\le n\) by (6), and \(\gcd(9,d)\mid n\) by (8). Hence there is a positive integer \(K_0\) such that
\[
d\mid K_0\qquad\text{and}\qquad D(K_0)=n. \tag{9}
\]
The number \(K_0\) already has the two required divisibility properties, but it could conceivably equal \(n\). We therefore enlarge it in a way that preserves both its digit sum and divisibility by \(d\). Define
\[
k=10^{n+1}K_0.
\]
Multiplication by \(10^{n+1}\) appends \(n+1\) zeros to the decimal expansion of \(K_0\), so it does not alter the sum of the digits. Thus, by (9),
\[
D(k)=D(K_0)=n. \tag{10}
\]
Also, since \(d\mid K_0\), we have
\[
d\mid k. \tag{11}
\]

We check that \(k\) is distinct from \(n\). Since \(K_0\ge1\),
\[
k=10^{n+1}K_0\ge10^{n+1}.
\]
For every nonnegative \(n\), one has \(10^{n+1}>n\) (for example, \(2^{n+1}\ge n+1>n\), and \(10^{n+1}\ge2^{n+1}\)). Hence
\[
k>n,
\]
so in particular \(k\neq n\). We also have \(k>0\).

Finally, recall that \(d=D(n)\). From (11),
\[
D(n)=d\mid k.
\]
From (10),
\[
D(k)=n\mid n.
\]
Therefore \(k\) is a positive Harshad amicable partner of \(n\), distinct from \(n\).

Thus, for every positive integer \(n\), the set
\[
\{k>0:k\neq n,\ D(n)\mid k,\ D(k)\mid n\}
\]
is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle it has a least element, and every element of this set is positive. The value \(a(n)\), defined to be this least element when the set is nonempty and to be \(0\) only when it is empty, is consequently positive. In particular,
\[
a(n)\neq0
\]
for every positive integer \(n\), as required.
